turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, in you come. Blood pressure's one twenty eight over seventy... no, sorry, one eighteen over seventy four, and your pulse is seventy two beats a minute. Pop yourself down.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Is one eighteen bad? I've been in a right state about it all morning.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): No, love, that's a normal blood pressure. My sister's was sky high last year and they started her on tablets, totally different kettle of fish.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She was up half the night googling. I told her it could wait till we actually got here.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Okonkwo. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, it's the sneezing. Every spring it kicks off and I just can't cope with it.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. Talk me through what actually happens.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Well my nose runs, my eyes itch like mad, and I sneeze all day. It happens every spring when the pollen's about.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been through a box of tissues a day since the trees came out. Keeps rubbing at her eyes.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this spring's bout been going on?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, about three weeks... no, actually it's been five weeks. I lost count.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Is this going to turn into asthma? My neighbour ended up in hospital and I've been panicking.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll get to that. Any wheeze, or a tight chest?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No wheeze. I keep listening and there's nothing.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough? Shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough, and I'm not breathless. Honestly.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Are you taking anything for it at the moment?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Citirizine. I take it sometimes, not every day. The packet says ten milligrams... no, hang on, mine are the five milligram ones. I checked this morning.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cetirizine, yes. The usual advice is once a day. So you're not doing that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only when the sneezing's really bad. Maybe three days a week? I'm not sure I stick to it properly.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else, prescribed or over the counter?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I tried a nasal spray years back, Beconase, but I stopped it.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): What made you stop?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): It stung my nose and I didn't think it was doing anything. That was ages ago.
[SEG0025] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, quick one. Peak flow outside was four hundred and twenty litres a minute. My own asthma's been grumbling with this pollen, I've had to up my inhaler.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Four twenty is a perfectly decent peak flow. Any allergies yourself, to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. My sister's allergic to dust, really badly, but I'm not. They tested me years ago.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her sister, not mine. I nearly chipped in that my little boy gets eczema, but that's nothing to do with her.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): The test, what did they actually tell you?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a blood test at the hospital. They said it was borderline for pollen. I never got the number, and I can't remember which year.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. We won't treat a borderline result we can't see as gospel. Let me look at your nose and eyes.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): The lining of your nose is pale and boggy. Your eyes are watery, but the whites aren't badly red.

[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): What's happening is pollen sticks to the lining and your body releases histamine. That histamine makes the lining swell and itch, and it sets off the sneezing. It isn't damaging the tissue.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Histamine? Is that dangerous long term? Am I damaging my nose every year? Sorry, I ask too much.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're not damaging it. Same chemical on the surface of the eyes, which is why they itch and water. Nothing I'm seeing suggests harm.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So I won't go blind or anything. I know that sounds daft.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): You won't. Any fever, or do you feel unwell in yourself?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I feel fine in myself, just fed up with the sneezing.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your tummy, your waterworks, any trouble there?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. All normal.

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. I think this is hay fever, seasonal allergic rhinitis. Cetirizine a few days a week isn't really holding it. I'd switch you to fexofenadine, one hundred and eighty milligrams, one tablet once a day by mouth, and add sodium cromoglicate eye drops.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Fexo-what? Will that make me drowsy? I drive to the office every day.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fexofenadine. It's a non-drowsy antihistamine. Stop the cetirizine when you start it, don't take both. The drops are one drop in each eye four times a day.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Four times a day, I'll forget, what if I miss one? And one hundred and eighty, isn't that huge? I read ten was the dose, wait, that was the citirizine, not this new one.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, ten was the figure on the old packet, and yours are five milligrams. One hundred and eighty is the normal adult dose of fexofenadine, not too much. If you miss a drop, just do the next one.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can remind her about the drops. I already do my dad's, he's got glaucoma, so I'm used to eye drops.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Are the drops safe with contact lenses? I wear them for work. And can this get worse every year? I was reading at two in the morning.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Take the lenses out, put the drop in, and leave them out for fifteen minutes. Screens and lenses can dry the eyes a bit but they don't cause this pattern. Try not to rub.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does work in an office, lots of screens. I keep saying take breaks.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like you back in four weeks so we can see if this has settled. Reception will book it.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks, okay. What if I get wheezy before then? Do I just wait?
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. If you start wheezing or you get breathless, come back sooner, don't wait the four weeks. Start both medicines today if the chemist has them.

spec.situation: Sneezing, itchy eyes and runny nose every spring; takes cetirizine 'sometimes'; sister is allergic to dust; no wheeze; doctor changes antihistamine and adds eye drops.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Completed blood test borderline for pollen supported; 'requested_by=patient' not stated.
bad.text: Pollen allergy blood test (type=laboratory, status=completed, requested_by=patient)

bad.reason: Explanation supported, but status isn't 'recommended' and responsible person isn't patient.
bad.text: Explained that pollen triggers histamine release, which swells and itches the nasal lining and causes sneezing, without damaging the tissue (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)
